facts.title: Born From a Green Flame
facts.text: Thallium was discovered in 1861 by the British chemist William Crookes, who spotted a brilliant, unexpected green line while examining residues from a sulfuric acid plant with a spectroscope. He named the element after the Greek word 'thallos', meaning a green shoot or twig, in honor of that vivid emerald spectral line. It was one of the first elements ever identified by spectroscopy rather than by classical chemical separation.

facts.title: A Discovery Claimed Twice
facts.text: Although Crookes detected thallium's spectral signature first, it was the French chemist Claude-Auguste Lamy who, in 1862, isolated a sizeable metallic ingot and characterized its properties. The two men disputed credit for years, and Lamy even exhibited his thallium metal at the 1862 London International Exhibition. Today both are usually credited, with Crookes recognized for the discovery and Lamy for the isolation.

facts.title: Soft Enough to Cut
facts.text: Pure thallium is a bluish-grey, remarkably soft metal that can be cut with a knife and marks paper much like lead. Freshly exposed surfaces are shiny but quickly tarnish to a dull grey oxide layer in moist air. With a melting point of about 304 degrees Celsius and a density around 11.85 grams per cubic centimeter, it is both heavy and easily worked.

facts.title: The Poisoner's Poison
facts.text: Thallium salts are colorless, odorless, tasteless, and highly toxic, earning the element a grim reputation in the history of crime. Thallium sulfate was once widely sold as a rat poison and ant killer until many countries banned it for household use in the mid-20th century because of accidental deaths. A lethal dose for an adult can be roughly one gram, and poisoning famously causes dramatic hair loss alongside nerve damage.

facts.title: A Detective's Lifesaver
facts.text: In 1977 the writer Agatha Christie's novel 'The Pale Horse' helped save a real life: a nurse recognized the symptoms of thallium poisoning she had read about in the book in a sick infant in London. Doctors confirmed the diagnosis and treated the child, who recovered. Thallium poisoning is now treated with Prussian blue, a pigment that binds the metal in the gut so it can be excreted.

facts.title: Two Faces, One Element
facts.text: Thallium shows an unusual chemistry because it forms stable compounds in two oxidation states: +1 (thallous) and +3 (thallic). The +1 state is exceptionally stable thanks to the 'inert pair effect', where its two outer 6s electrons resist bonding. In the +1 form, thallium chemically mimics potassium and is taken up by the body through the same channels, which is precisely why it is so insidiously toxic.

facts.title: Imaging the Living Heart
facts.text: A radioactive isotope, thallium-201, became a cornerstone of nuclear cardiology because the body treats it like potassium and concentrates it in healthy, well-perfused heart muscle. In a thallium stress test, doctors track its gamma emissions to map blood flow and reveal areas damaged by a heart attack or starved by blocked arteries. Thallium-201 has a half-life of about 73 hours, convenient for medical imaging.

facts.title: Seeing in the Dark
facts.text: Thallium dramatically extends how far into the infrared we can see. Crystals of thallium bromide-iodide, sold under the trade name KRS-5, transmit long-wavelength infrared light and are used in spectroscopy and thermal optics. Thallium-doped sodium iodide crystals are also workhorse scintillation detectors, flashing with light when struck by gamma rays in everything from medical scanners to airport security.

facts.title: Hidden in Sulfide Ores
facts.text: Thallium is not especially rare in the crust, at roughly 0.7 parts per million, but it almost never forms its own ore deposits. Instead it hides as a trace impurity inside the sulfide minerals of copper, lead, zinc, and iron, and it is recovered chiefly as a byproduct of smelting those metals and from flue dusts. Rare thallium minerals such as crookesite and lorandite do exist but are collector's curiosities.

facts.title: A Superconducting Surprise
facts.text: Thallium-based copper-oxide ceramics are among the higher-temperature superconductors known, with some thallium-barium-calcium-copper-oxide compounds losing all electrical resistance above 120 kelvin. That is well above the boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen at 77 kelvin, which makes such materials attractive for research. In a very different role, thallium-mercury alloys stay liquid down to about minus 60 degrees Celsius, useful in extreme-cold thermometers.
